cse-2016-2-cs-13.approach: Evaluate each algorithm on already-sorted input with its standard textbook implementation, then pick the option whose set of true statements matches.

steps.title: Quicksort (I)
steps.body: With the standard first/last-element pivot, sorted input makes every partition maximally unbalanced: sizes $n-1$ and $0$. So $T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n^2)$. **I is true.**

steps.title: Merge sort (III)
steps.body: Merge sort always splits in half and merges every level: $T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$ regardless of input order. **III is false.**

steps.title: Insertion sort (IV)
steps.body: Each new element is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put: $n-1$ comparisons, $\Theta(n)$. **IV is true.**

steps.title: Bubble sort (II) and the option
steps.body: Bubble sort with the usual "no swaps in a pass ⇒ stop" check finishes after one pass, $\Theta(n)$, so II is not claimed. The true set is $\{\text{I},\text{IV}\}$ → option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: II assumes the unoptimised bubble sort; with the early-exit flag it is $\Theta(n)$ on sorted input.
III is false: merge sort is $\Theta(n\log n)$ on every input.
Drops I, which is true (end-pivot quicksort is $\Theta(n^2)$ on sorted input), and keeps II, which fails for bubble sort with the early-exit check.
I (unbalanced partitions) and IV (one comparison per element) are both true.

pitfalls: Thinking merge sort adapts to sorted input — it does not.
Forgetting that sorted input is the worst case for end-pivot quicksort.
cse-2016-2-cs-13.verification: Matches the GATE 2016 (Set 2) answer key, which lists (D); the stored key (C) was corrected.

cse-2016-2-cs-14.approach: Floyd-Warshall fills a table $d^{(k)}[i][j]$ from $d^{(k-1)}$ using optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems — the defining traits of dynamic programming.

steps.title: The recurrence
steps.body: $d^{(k)}_{ij}=\min\left(d^{(k-1)}_{ij},\ d^{(k-1)}_{ik}+d^{(k-1)}_{kj}\right)$: the best path using intermediates $\{1,\dots,k\}$ is built from best paths using $\{1,\dots,k-1\}$.

steps.title: Classify it
steps.body: Subproblem answers are stored and reused $\Theta(n)$ times each, filled bottom-up in $\Theta(n^3)$ — this is **dynamic programming**, option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: No locally-optimal irreversible choice is made (that is Dijkstra/Prim style).
Subproblems overlap heavily; they are not independent halves combined once.
Tabulated recurrence over intermediate vertex sets — DP.
It clearly fits DP, so "none" is wrong.

cse-2016-2-cs-14.verification: Standard classification (CLRS ch. 25 presents it as a DP algorithm).

cse-2016-2-cs-15.approach: Cost each operation on a sorted doubly linked list (no random access), multiply by how many times it is done, and add; the decrease-key term dominates.
cse-2016-2-cs-15.given:
| Operation | Count | Cost each | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| delete (pointer given) | $\Theta(N)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(N)$ |
| insert | $O(\log N)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N\log N)$ |
| find | $O(\log N)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N\log N)$ |
| decrease-key (pointer given) | $\Theta(N)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N^2)$ |

steps.title: Per-operation cost
steps.body:
- **delete** with a pointer: relink prev/next, $O(1)$.
- **insert** into a sorted list: walk to the position, $O(N)$ (no binary search on a list).
- **find**: linear scan, $O(N)$.
- **decrease-key** with a pointer: the key shrinks, so the node may have to move left past up to $N$ nodes to keep the list sorted, $O(N)$.

steps.title: Add up
steps.body: $$O(N)\cdot 1+O(\log N)\cdot O(N)+O(\log N)\cdot O(N)+\Theta(N)\cdot O(N)=O(N)+O(N\log N)+O(N^2)=O(N^2).$$ Option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Ignores that a single find or decrease-key on a list is already linear.
Would need decrease-key in $O(1)$, but the node must be repositioned to keep the list sorted.
The $\Theta(N)$ decrease-keys at $O(N)$ each dominate: $O(N^2)$.
Over-counts: no term contributes $N^2\log N$.

pitfalls: Assuming binary search works on a sorted linked list.
Treating decrease-key as $O(1)$ because a pointer is given — the pointer saves the search, not the re-positioning.
cse-2016-2-cs-15.verification: Dominant term check: $N\cdot N=N^2$ exceeds $N\log N$ for large $N$.

cse-2016-2-cs-16.approach: Simplify the regular expression first: it denotes every string of length at least 1, which needs exactly two DFA states.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body: $(0+1)^*(0+1)(0+1)^*$ requires one symbol in the middle with anything around it, so it is $(0+1)^+$: all **non-empty** strings over $\{0,1\}$.

steps.title: Build and minimise the DFA
steps.body: State $q_0$ (start, non-accepting, "nothing read") goes to $q_1$ on 0 or 1; $q_1$ (accepting) loops on 0,1. $\varepsilon$ is rejected and every other string accepted, so $q_0\not\equiv q_1$ — they cannot merge, and one state cannot do it. Minimum = **2**.

pitfalls: Counting the three factors of the expression as three states.
Forgetting that the language excludes $\varepsilon$, so the start state cannot accept.
cse-2016-2-cs-16.verification: Myhill–Nerode: classes are $\{\varepsilon\}$ and all non-empty strings — exactly two.

cse-2016-2-cs-17.approach: Write each language explicitly: $L_1=\{a^nb^n\}$ needs unbounded counting (not regular), while $L_2=(ab)^*$ is plainly regular.

steps.title: Identify the languages
steps.body: $S_1\to aS_1b\mid\varepsilon$ gives $L_1=\{a^nb^n: n\ge 0\}$. $S_2\to abS_2\mid\varepsilon$ gives $L_2=\{(ab)^n: n\ge0\}=(ab)^*$.

steps.title: Decide regularity
steps.body: $L_1$: pump $a^pb^p$ — any $y$ inside the first $p$ symbols is all $a$'s, so $xy^2z$ has more $a$'s than $b$'s. Not regular, **P false**. $L_2=(ab)^*$ is a regular expression (also a right-linear grammar), **Q true**. Option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $L_1=a^nb^n$ is the classic non-regular language.
Reversed: it is $L_1$ that is non-regular and $L_2$ that is regular.
P is false, Q is true.
$L_2=(ab)^*$ is regular; the grammar is right-linear.

cse-2016-2-cs-17.verification: $S_2\to abS_2$ is right-linear, which always generates a regular language.

cse-2016-2-cs-18.approach: Use two facts per statement: what class the complemented language falls in, and what that class is closed under.

steps.title: I and II
steps.body:
**I:** recursive languages are closed under complement, so $\overline{L_3}$ is recursive ⊆ RE; RE is closed under union ⇒ $\overline{L_3}\cup L_4$ is RE. **True.**

**II:** every CFL is recursive (membership is decidable, e.g. CYK), so $\overline{L_2}$ is recursive; recursive ∪ recursive is recursive. **True.**

steps.title: III and IV
steps.body:
**III:** $L_1^*$ is regular (closure under star); CFL ∩ regular is a CFL. **True.**

**IV:** CFLs are not closed under complement, so $\overline{L_2}$ need not be context-free; e.g. $L_1=\varnothing$ and $L_2=\overline{\{a^nb^nc^n\}}$ (a CFL) give $L_1\cup\overline{L_2}=\{a^nb^nc^n\}$, not a CFL. **False.**

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: True set $=\{\text{I},\text{II},\text{III}\}$ → option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Misses II and III, both of which follow from standard closure facts.
Misses II: a CFL’s complement is still recursive.
IV is false — CFLs are not closed under complement.
Exactly I, II and III hold.

pitfalls: Confusing "complement of a CFL is not always CFL" with "not decidable" — it is always recursive.
cse-2016-2-cs-18.verification: Counterexample for IV checked: $\overline{\{a^nb^nc^n\}}$ is a known CFL, and its complement is not.

cse-2016-2-cs-19.approach: Map each compiler phase to the tool or artefact it is built on.

steps.title: Front-end phases
steps.body:
- **Lexical analysis** — tokens are specified by **regular expressions** (iii).
- **Top-down parsing** — traces a **leftmost derivation** (i).

steps.title: Later phases and the option
steps.body:
- **Semantic analysis** — performs **type checking** (ii).
- **Runtime environment** — manages **activation records** (iv).

P–iii, Q–i, R–ii, S–iv → option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Lexical analysis does not use leftmost derivations, and semantic analysis does not manage activation records.
All four pairs are correct.
Type checking is semantic, not lexical; top-down parsing is not regular-expression matching.
Lexical analysis is not about activation records; runtime environments are not regular expressions.

cse-2016-2-cs-19.verification: Only (B) has Q–i and R–ii together with P–iii.

cse-2016-2-cs-20.approach: Increasing frames can increase faults (Belady’s anomaly) only for algorithms that are not stack algorithms; FIFO is the classic one.

steps.title: Stack algorithms are safe
steps.body: LRU and OPT are **stack algorithms**: the set of pages held with $k$ frames is always a subset of those held with $k+1$ frames, so faults can never rise with more frames.

steps.title: FIFO shows the anomaly
steps.body: On $1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5$ FIFO gives **9** faults with 3 frames but **10** with 4 frames. Option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: LRU is a stack algorithm — immune to Belady’s anomaly.
OPT is a stack algorithm and optimal for every frame count.
MRU is also a stack algorithm (priority by recency), so it does not suffer the anomaly; FIFO is the intended answer.
FIFO exhibits Belady’s anomaly.

cse-2016-2-cs-20.verification: Counted the classic reference string: 9 faults (3 frames) vs 10 faults (4 frames).

cse-2016-2-cs-21.approach: A B+ tree grows and shrinks only at the root, so every leaf is always at the same depth — that is what "balanced" means for it.

steps.title: How the height changes
steps.body: Insertions split full nodes and push a key **up**; only when the root splits is a new root created, deepening every leaf by one together. Deletions merge nodes and remove a level only at the root.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Height changes only at the root, hence all root-to-leaf paths have **equal** length → option **(A)**.

answer.value: All root-to-leaf paths are equal — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Exactly the B+ tree invariant: every leaf is at the same depth.
That is the AVL-style height-balance idea, not the B+ tree property.
Fan-out of siblings can differ widely (anything between ⌈m/2⌉ and m).
Leaf occupancy can differ widely too (half-full to full).

cse-2016-2-cs-21.verification: Insertion/deletion only change height at the root, so depths remain identical.

cse-2016-2-cs-22.approach: An edge $T_i\to T_j$ means $T_i$ must precede $T_j$; for an acyclic graph a topological order respects every such edge, giving an equivalent serial schedule.

steps.title: What the edges mean
steps.body: A conflict edge $T_i\to T_j$ says some operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before one of $T_j$, so $T_i$ must come first in any equivalent serial order.

steps.title: Order the vertices
steps.body: $S$ serializable ⇒ graph is acyclic ⇒ a topological order exists and puts every $T_i$ before each $T_j$ it points to. Option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Respects every precedence edge.
A DFS visiting order can list a vertex before its predecessor (only reverse post-order is safe).
BFS order from a vertex can also violate edges, e.g. reaching $T_j$ before another predecessor $T_k$.
Indices carry no information about conflicts.

cse-2016-2-cs-22.verification: Example: edges $T_2\to T_1$ — ascending index order $T_1,T_2$ would be wrong; topological order gives $T_2,T_1$.

cse-2016-2-cs-23.approach: A signature is created with the signer’s private key, so anyone verifies it with the signer’s public key.

steps.title: Signing
steps.body: Anarkali signs with her **private** key: $\sigma=\text{Sign}(K^{-}_{A},\ h(m))$; only she can produce it.

steps.title: Verifying
steps.body: Salim checks $\text{Verify}(K^{+}_{A},\ \sigma)=h(m)$ — he needs **Anarkali's public key**. Option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: The signer’s public key undoes the private-key signing.
Salim’s public key is for encrypting messages to Salim, not for verifying Anarkali.
Salim’s private key decrypts messages sent to him; it plays no role in her signature.
Anarkali’s private key is secret — only she has it, and it is used to sign.

cse-2016-2-cs-23.verification: Signature verification must be possible for anyone, so it can only need a public key — the sender’s.

cse-2016-2-cs-24.approach: Check each statement against CSMA/CD as used in classic Ethernet.

steps.title: Test each statement
steps.body:
- (A) A station keeps sensing while sending — that is how it detects collisions. False.
- (B) The jam signal tells all stations a collision occurred; padding is done by the PAD field. False.
- (C) On detecting a collision the station aborts, sends a jam signal and backs off. False.

steps.title: Check D
steps.body: (D) After the $n$-th collision a wait of $K\cdot 51.2\,\mu s$ with $K\in\{0,\dots,2^{\min(n,10)}-1\}$ is chosen at random; the growing range makes repeat collisions less likely. **True** → **(D)**.

answer.value: Exponential backoff reduces repeat collisions — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: Carrier sensing continues during transmission for collision detection.
Jamming announces a collision; short frames are padded by the PAD field.
The station stops transmitting once a collision is detected.
Random waits drawn from a doubling range spread retransmissions apart.

cse-2016-2-cs-24.verification: Each false statement contradicts a defining CSMA/CD rule.

cse-2016-2-cs-25.approach: Follow what a freshly booted host must do: resolve the name, open the TCP connection, then send the HTTP request.

steps.title: Name resolution first
steps.body: After a restart the DNS cache is empty, so the host first sends a **DNS query** for the server's IP address.

steps.title: Connect, then request
steps.body:
1. With the IP, open a TCP connection: **TCP SYN** (three-way handshake).
2. On the established connection send the **HTTP GET**.

Option **(C)**.

answer.value: DNS query, TCP SYN, HTTP GET — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: HTTP needs an open TCP connection and an IP address first.
The HTTP GET cannot go before the TCP SYN.
Resolve, connect, request — correct order.
SYN needs the destination IP, which DNS supplies.

pitfalls: ARP for the gateway also happens, but it is not among the listed packets.
cse-2016-2-cs-25.verification: Each step depends on the previous one’s result (IP address, then connection).

cse-2016-2-cs-26.approach: Reflexivity is immediate ($a\le a$); for transitivity find a chain where the "or" is satisfied by different coordinates in each link.

steps.title: P: reflexive
steps.body: $(a,b)R(a,b)$ since $a\le a$. **P true.**

steps.title: Q: transitive? — counterexample
steps.body: $(3,2)R(1,3)$ because $2\le 3$; $(1,3)R(2,1)$ because $1\le 2$. But $(3,2)R(2,1)$ needs $3\le 2$ or $2\le 1$ — both false. **Q false.** Option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Q fails on the chain $(3,2),(1,3),(2,1)$.
Reflexive holds and transitivity fails.
P is true, not false.
P is true.

pitfalls: With "and" instead of "or" the relation would be transitive (product order) — the "or" breaks it.
cse-2016-2-cs-26.verification: Re-checked each link of the counterexample numerically.

cse-2016-2-cs-27.approach: Test each formula with the standard quantifier laws; a two-element domain where $p$ and $q$ split the elements kills (D).

steps.title: A, B, C are valid
steps.body:
- (A) $\forall x\,p\Rightarrow\forall x\,q\equiv\neg\forall x\,p\vee\forall x\,q\equiv\exists x\,\neg p\vee\forall x\,q$ — an implication between equivalent formulas: valid.
- (B) $\exists x\,p\vee\exists x\,q\equiv\exists x(p\vee q)$: valid.
- (C) A witness of $p\wedge q$ is a witness for each: valid.

steps.title: D fails
steps.body: Domain $\{1,2\}$, $p=\{1\}$, $q=\{2\}$: $\forall x(p\vee q)$ is true, but $\forall x\,p$ and $\forall x\,q$ are both false. So (D) is **not valid** → option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Valid: the consequent is just a rewriting of the antecedent.
Valid: $\exists$ distributes over $\vee$.
Valid: one witness satisfies both conjuncts.
$\forall$ does not distribute over $\vee$ — counterexample above.

cse-2016-2-cs-27.verification: The counter-model makes the antecedent of D true and its consequent false.

cse-2016-2-cs-28.approach: Model compounds as vertices and reactions as edges; the handshake lemma forces the degree sum in $U\setminus S$ to be odd.

steps.title: Degree sum
steps.body: Sum of all degrees $=2|E|$ is even. Vertices in $S$ contribute $9\times 3=27$ (odd).

steps.title: Parity of the rest
steps.body: So $\sum_{v\in U\setminus S}\deg v=\text{even}-27=\text{odd}$. An odd sum needs at least one odd term ⇒ **II always true**. I and III are not forced (the 14 vertices may have a mix of parities, e.g. one odd and the rest even, or three odd). Option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Only the number of odd-degree vertices is forced to be odd, not all of them.
The odd degree-sum forces at least one odd vertex.
Impossible: all even would make the sum even.
II is always true.

cse-2016-2-cs-28.verification: Number of odd-degree vertices overall is even: 9 in $S$ ⇒ an odd number in $U\setminus S$, hence ≥ 1.

cse-2016-2-cs-29.approach: Use $13\equiv -4\pmod{17}$; its powers cycle quickly ($(-4)^2=16\equiv-1$), so reduce the exponent mod 4.

cse-2016-2-cs-30.approach: Feed the $F$ units as early as possible: the two $U_G$ units produce two results every 3 ns, faster than the two $U_F$ units consume them (two every 5 ns), so $F$ is the bottleneck and only the first $G$ delay is exposed.

steps.title: Schedule the G computations
steps.body: Two at a time: $G$ pairs finish at $3,6,9,12,15$ ns.

scene.caption: G results ready in pairs at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 ns

steps.title: Schedule the F computations
steps.body: Each $U_F$ takes 5 jobs back to back. First pair starts at 3 (inputs ready), then $8,13,18,23$ — every input is ready well before (latest needed at 23, ready at 15). Last pair ends at $23+5=28$ ns.

scene.caption: F units busy from 3 to 28 ns without idling

steps.title: Lower bound confirms it
steps.body: No $F$ can start before $3$ ns, and the $U_F$ units need $10\times5/2=25$ ns of work each pair-wise: $3+25=28$. Minimum time **28 ns**.

pitfalls: Adding $3+5$ per item and dividing by 2 ($40$ ns) ignores overlap of G and F.
Using $15+5=20$ forgets that F is the slower stage.
cse-2016-2-cs-30.verification: Lower bound $3+25=28$ is achieved by the schedule, so it is optimal.

cse-2016-2-cs-31.approach: Add the bit widths of all fields, round up to whole bytes, multiply by 100.

steps.title: Field widths
steps.body: Opcode: $\lceil\log_2 12\rceil=4$ bits. Each register id: $\log_2 64=6$ bits, three of them $=18$. Immediate $=12$. Total $=4+18+12=34$ bits.

steps.title: Byte-align and multiply
steps.body: $\lceil 34/8\rceil=5$ bytes per instruction, so $100\times5=$ **500** bytes.

pitfalls: Using $34/8=4.25$ bytes ⇒ 425 — byte alignment forces 5 bytes.

cse-2016-2-cs-32.approach: Index + offset bits always equal $\log_2(\text{cache size}/\text{associativity})$, so the block size cancels and tag = address bits minus that.

steps.title: Index + offset
steps.body: Let block $=2^b$ bytes. Sets $=\dfrac{2^{19}}{8\cdot 2^b}=2^{16-b}$ ⇒ index $=16-b$, offset $=b$, so index + offset $=16$ bits for **any** block size.

cse-2016-2-cs-32.verification: With 64 B blocks: offset 6, sets $2^{19}/(8\cdot64)=1024$ ⇒ index 10; $40-10-6=24$ ✓.

cse-2016-2-cs-33.approach: Express all stage delays with one unit, use the 3 GHz clock to fix the unit, split the longest stage and take the new maximum.

steps.title: Ratio of stages
steps.body: $\tau_1=\tfrac34\tau_2=2\tau_3$. Put $\tau_1=6$: $\tau_2=8$, $\tau_3=3$. Longest stage $\tau_2=8$ units.

steps.title: Fix the unit from 3 GHz
steps.body: Clock period $=1/3$ ns $=8$ units ⇒ 1 unit $=\tfrac{1}{24}$ ns.

pitfalls: Splitting $\tau_1$ (looks first in the equation) instead of the largest stage $\tau_2$.
Doubling the frequency to 6 GHz — the new bottleneck is $\tau_1$, not half of $\tau_2$.

cse-2016-2-cs-34.approach: In a min-heap every ancestor of 9 is smaller than 9, so at most 8 ancestors fit: depth ≤ 8; and a chain $1\to2\to\dots\to9$ achieves it since the heap has depths 0–9.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: Heap order: every ancestor of 9 holds a smaller key. Only $1,\dots,8$ are smaller, so 9 has at most 8 ancestors ⇒ depth $\le 8$.

steps.title: It is achievable
steps.body: $1023=2^{10}-1$ nodes ⇒ a perfect tree with depths $0..9$. Place $1,2,\dots,8$ down one path and 9 as the child of 8 (depth 8); fill every other slot with $10,\dots,1023$ in heap order. All heap conditions hold. Maximum depth = **8**.

pitfalls: Answering 9 (the tree height) — 9 would then need 9 smaller ancestors.
cse-2016-2-cs-34.verification: Depth 8 < height 9, so the chain fits; depth 9 would need 9 keys below 9 — impossible.
